abstract: Inaugural post in "Street Level," a commentary series by Kartik B. Athreya, Director of Research at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It is a thematic synthesis of recent New York Fed research on AI and the labor market rather than an original empirical study, and its central claim is that AI's labor-market impact so far "has more to do with changing skill requirements than eliminating jobs." Athreya assembles three strands: an October 2024 finding that individuals exposed to generative AI held bleaker expectations for job availability and income inequality; a September 2025 regional-survey result that AI adoption is rising quickly while firms report very few AI-driven layoffs; and survey evidence that firms overwhelmingly intend to retrain rather than fire workers. The single numeric table reports Second District adoption from the NY Fed Regional Business Surveys (August 2025): share of service firms using AI rose from 25 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025 with 44 percent expected within six months, and manufacturers from 16 percent to 26 percent with 33 percent expected. The post closes with two speculative observations: that occupational specialization leaves workers exposed to a sudden collapse in the value of a narrow skill set, and that AI's demand-side effects — cheaper goods plus a tilt toward status-driven, positional consumption — may prove more consequential in the long run than its supply-side absorption.
keyFindings: 40 percent of Second District service firms reported using AI in 2025, up from 25 percent in 2024, with 44 percent expected within the next six months (NY Fed Regional Business Surveys, August 2025).
26 percent of Second District manufacturers reported using AI in 2025, up from 16 percent in 2024, with 33 percent expected within the next six months.
Firms report "very few AI-driven layoffs" despite rapidly rising adoption; AI is instead reshaping hiring and skill needs.
Firms anticipate more reductions in hiring plans going forward, especially for college-educated workers.
Firms "overwhelmingly intend to retrain workers rather than fire them" as they adopt AI; the supporting retraining chart reports no labeled values in the post text.
Individuals exposed to generative AI tools as of October 2024 held bleaker expectations for job availability and income inequality.
methodology: Editorial synthesis by the NY Fed's Director of Research, drawing on previously published Liberty Street Economics posts, the NY Fed Regional Business Surveys (August 2024 and August 2025 special-topic modules covering the Second District: New York State, northern New Jersey, and Fairfield County, Connecticut), and the Survey of Consumer Expectations. No new data collection, no original estimation, and no causal identification strategy. The adoption figures are firm self-reports of AI use, with the forward-looking column being firm expectations rather than measurement.
qualifiers: Tier 2 rather than Tier 1: this is signed commentary that explicitly frames itself as "adding my own observations," not peer-reviewed research or a primary statistical release, even though other Liberty Street Economics posts in this corpus that present original analysis are registered at Tier 1. All statistics here are restatements of previously published work. The adoption table is regional, not national — the Second District is not the United States — and it is therefore not comparable to the Census BTOS national series that jobsdata plots, which stood at 17.9 percent on a different and narrower instrument. The 2025 figures also come from an August 2025 survey, roughly a year older than the post itself. The retraining chart is presented without labeled values in the text, so no retraining percentage can be quoted. Every claim about layoffs and hiring is qualitative in this post; no layoff or displacement rate is stated. Athreya's closing observations on specialization risk and positional consumption are explicitly speculative and carry no supporting estimates.
